title: Making Decisions with if / elif / else
summary: Teach your program to choose: run different code depending on whether a condition is True or False.

certification.description: Make decisions and branch the flow with the if instruction (conditional statements: if, if-else, if-elif, if-elif-else).

cards.title: Programs that choose
cards.body:
So far your programs ran every line, top to bottom. Real programs need to **decide**.

An `if` statement checks a **condition** — an expression that is either `True` or `False`. If it is `True`, the indented block underneath runs. If not, Python skips it.

```python
if condition:
    # runs only when condition is True
elif other_condition:
    # checked only if the first one was False
else:
    # runs when nothing above matched
```

Python checks the branches **in order** and runs **only the first one that matches** — then jumps past the whole block.
keyPoints: A condition is any expression that evaluates to True or False, e.g. `age >= 18`.
Every `if`, `elif` and `else` line ends with a colon `:`.
The code inside a branch is indented by 4 spaces — indentation is how Python knows what belongs to the branch.
`=` stores a value; `==` compares two values.
Branches are checked top to bottom; only the first True branch runs.

realWorld.title: Why this matters in the real world
realWorld.body: Every checkout page you have ever used runs code like this. *Is the customer a member? Is the basket over the free-shipping threshold? Is the card country different from the shipping country (possible fraud)?* Banks, airlines and e-commerce sites encode thousands of business rules as `if / elif / else` chains — and getting the **order** of the checks wrong is one of the most common, costly bugs in production software.

cards.title: Walkthrough: a weather advisor
cards.expectedOutput:
Hot day - stay hydrated!
Forecast done.

steps.explanation: We store the number `31` in a variable called `temperature`.
`temperature >= 30` evaluates to `True` (31 is at least 30), so the indented `print` on line 4 runs.
`elif` means *else if*. Because the first branch already matched, Python **skips this check entirely** — even though 31 >= 18 is also True.
`else` has no condition: it is the fallback when nothing above matched. Skipped here too.
This line is **not indented**, so it is outside the `if` block and always runs. Try changing `temperature` to `12` and press **Run**!

challenge.title: Free-shipping rules
challenge.prompt:
You're building the checkout for an online store. Complete the function `shipping_cost(order_total, is_member)` so it **returns** the right shipping fee.

The last two lines read an order total typed by the customer and print the fee for a non-member — don't change them.
requirements: Orders of **$50 or more** ship free (`0`).
Orders of **$20 or more** (but under $50) cost `4.99`.
challenge.starterCode:
def shipping_cost(order_total, is_member):
    # TODO: return the correct shipping fee
    return 0


total = float(input())
print(f"Shipping: ${shipping_cost(total, False):.2f}")

hints.text: Check the rules in order from the most specific (members) to the most general (everything else).
Is $50 itself free? "$50 or more" means you need `>=`, not `>`.

Skeleton:
```python
if is_member:
    return 0
elif order_total >= 50:
    ...
```

tests.name: Members always ship free
tests.code:
assert shipping_cost(10, True) == 0
assert shipping_cost(99, True) == 0
tests.failureHint: Check `is_member` first, before looking at the order total.

tests.name: Small orders cost 7.99
tests.code:
assert shipping_cost(19.99, False) == 7.99
assert shipping_cost(0.5, False) == 7.99

tests.name: Just under $50 is not free
tests.failureHint: Are your checks in the right order? The $50 rule must be tested before the $20 rule.

tests.name: Prints the fee for a $12.50 order
Prints the fee for a large order

questions.explanation: 85 fails `>= 90`, then passes `>= 80`, so `B` prints. The `>= 70` branch is never checked — only the first matching branch runs.

questions.prompt: Which line correctly checks whether `x` equals 10?
questions.explanation: `==` compares, `=` assigns. And every `if` line must end with a colon.

questions.prompt: Complete the code so it prints "teen" for ages 13–19.
questions.template:
age = 15
if age < 13:
    print("child")
___ age < 20:
    print("teen")
___:
    print("adult")
questions.explanation: `elif` adds another condition; `else` is the fallback and takes no condition.

questions.prompt: How many lines does this print?
questions.explanation: These are **two separate** `if` statements (the second starts with `if`, not `elif`), so both are checked: "big" and "medium" print.
